latin.631: §. II. Manducationem in S. Cœna duplicem, Propriam & Impropriam, Corporalem & Spiritualem, utramque æquè veram, ob duplicem inibì exhibitum proprium & improprium, Corporalem & Spiritualem, æquè verum utrobique cibum, panem nempe & Corpus Christi, ab Institutore S. Cœnæ, injunctam nobis esse, pia semper credidit antiquitas.
latin.632: Totius hujus nomine, Augustinum in compendio introducit pontificius quidam, ast sobrius Autor moderatusque, sæpius citatus Petrus Picherellus, cujus verba hîc recensuisse nemini ingratum accidere poterit; ita verò ille, Opusc. Theol. p. 176. in fine usque ad p. 178. in med. Augustinus profecto, ait, duas illas res in Cœnæ sacramento intelligens, diversos illius manducandi modos facit, de verbis Domini in Evangelium secundum Matth. & multis aliis locis, passim per antithesin explicat.
latin.633: Ut de verbis Apost. serm. 2. esse in Cœna aliquid quod spiritualiter manducatur, spiritualiter bibitur, & in Joh. tract. 26. esse carnem & sanguinem, & esse carnis & sanguinis sacramentum, & de verbis Apostoli serm. 2. esse aliud sacramentum, aliud virtutem sacramenti, esse aliquid quod sumitur in sacramento, & esse aliquid, quod ipsâ (Sacramenti) veritate manducatur & bibitur. in Johann. tractat. 59. Panem Domini manducare, & panem Dominum manducare, in Psal. 98. visibiliter celebrari sacramentum & Spiritualiter intelligi Sacramentum Epist. ad Cæsar. Ipsum corpus manducare, & non ipsum corpus manducare: Ipsum invisibiliter, & non ipsum visibiliter, in Johan. tract. 26.
latin.634: Carnaliter & visibiliter premere dentibus Sacramentum corporis & sanguinis Christi, & Spiritualiter manducare carnem ejus & bibere sanguinem ejus, de civitat. Dei lib. 21. cap. 15. Sacramento tenus, Corpus Christi manducare & sanguinem ejus bibere, & revera corpus Christi manducare & sanguinem ejus bibere. In Johan. tractat. 26. Sacramento corpus Christi manducare, & reipsâ Corpus Christi manducare. Manducare panem foris, & manducare panem intus. Premere panem dente, & manducare panem in corde, ibid. In Sacramento Carnem Christi edere, & Sanguinem Christi bibere, & in Johan. tract. 27. usque ad Spiritus participationem carnem Christi edere & Sanguinem ejus bibere, ut in Domini corpore tanquam membra maneamus. In Johan. tract. 26. quosdam pertinere ad visibile Sacramentum & quosdam pertinere ad virtutem Sacramenti, aliud esse Sacramentum, & Corpus & Sanguinem Christi, ad inquisit. Januarii cap. 3. qui visibilis est cibus, aliud esse Sacramentum in Johan. tract. 26. aliud virtutem Sacramenti in Psal. 77 secundum quam dicitur panis cælestis spiritualiter manducari, contra Max. lib. 3. cap. 12.
latin.635: Augustino adstipulatur Lutherus variis in locis Postillæ suæ Ecclesiasticæ, Concione in Epist. Dominicalem Septuagesima & in Evangelium festi Corporis Christi, in cap. 6 Johan. Vide Neodorpii Lutherum Orthodoxum à pag. 120.

pass_a.631: §. II. That a double Eating in the Sacred Supper — Proper and Improper, Corporal and Spiritual, each equally true — has been enjoined on us by the Institutor of the Sacred Supper on account of the double food exhibited there, proper and improper, Corporal and Spiritual, equally true on both sides, namely bread and Christ’s Body: this pious antiquity has always believed.
pass_a.632: In the name of this whole matter a certain pontifical yet sober and moderate Author often cited, Petrus Picherellus, introduces Augustine in summary — whose words it will be welcome to no one not to have reviewed here; so indeed he, Opusc. Theol. p. 176 at the end through p. 178 in the middle: Augustine certainly, he says, understanding those two things in the Supper’s sacrament, makes diverse modes of eating it, and from the Lord’s words in the Gospel according to Matthew and in many other places explains them everywhere by antithesis.
pass_a.633: As from the Apostle’s words serm. 2: that in the Supper there is something which is spiritually eaten, spiritually drunk; and in Joh. tract. 26: that there is flesh and blood, and that there is the sacrament of flesh and blood; and from the Apostle’s words serm. 2: that the sacrament is one thing, the virtue of the sacrament another; that there is something which is taken in the sacrament, and something which is eaten and drunk by the sacrament’s own truth. In Johann. tract. 59: to eat the Lord’s bread, and to eat the Lord as bread; in Psal. 98 / Epist. to Caesar: the sacrament celebrated visibly and the Sacrament understood Spiritually. To eat the body itself, and not to eat the body itself: the itself invisibly, and not the itself visibly — Joh. tract. 26.
pass_a.634: To press carnally and visibly with the teeth the Sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, and Spiritually to eat His flesh and drink His blood — City of God bk. 21 ch. 15. As far as the Sacrament, to eat Christ’s Body and drink His blood, and really to eat Christ’s body and drink His blood. In Joh. tract. 26: to eat Christ’s body by the Sacrament, and in the thing itself to eat Christ’s Body. To eat bread outside, and to eat bread inside. To press bread with the tooth, and to eat bread in the heart, ibid. In the Sacrament to eat Christ’s Flesh and drink Christ’s Blood, and in Joh. tract. 27 to eat Christ’s flesh and drink His Blood unto participation of the Spirit, that we may remain in the Lord’s body as members. In Joh. tract. 26: some pertain to the visible Sacrament and some to the Sacrament’s virtue; that the Sacrament is one thing and Christ’s Body and Blood another — to Januarius’s inquiry ch. 3 — which visible food is one thing, the Sacrament another (Joh. tract. 26), the Sacrament’s virtue another (Psal. 77) according to which the heavenly bread is said to be eaten spiritually — against Max. bk. 3 ch. 12.
pass_a.635: Luther agrees with Augustine in various places of his Ecclesiastical Postil, the Sermon on the Septuagesima Sunday Epistle and on the Gospel of the feast of Christ’s Body, and on John ch. 6. See Neodorpius’s Orthodox Luther from p. 120.

631: §.II: pious antiquity always held that the Sacred Supper enjoins a double eating — Proper and Improper, Corporal and Spiritual — each equally true.
The reason is the double food exhibited there, equally true on both sides: bread and Christ’s Body, from the Supper’s Institutor.
632: For this whole point the sober pontifical author Petrus Picherellus (often cited) brings Augustine in summary — Opusc. Theol. pp. 176–178.
Augustine, seeing two things in the Supper’s sacrament, makes diverse modes of eating and explains them by antithesis across Matthew and many other places.
633: Augustine’s antitheses (via Picherellus): something spiritually eaten and drunk; flesh and blood vs their sacrament; sacrament vs the sacrament’s virtue; what is taken in the sacrament vs what is eaten in the sacrament’s truth.
Further: eat the Lord’s bread vs eat the Lord as bread; sacrament celebrated visibly vs understood spiritually; eat the body itself vs not; invisibly vs visibly (Joh. tracts).
634: Teeth press the sacrament carnally/visibly vs spiritually eat flesh and drink blood (City of God 21.15). Sacramento tenus vs really; by sacrament vs in the thing itself; bread outside vs inside; tooth vs heart.

Eat unto Spirit-participation so we remain members in the Lord’s body. Some belong to the visible sacrament, some to its virtue — visible food / sacrament / virtue distinguished; heavenly bread eaten spiritually (Psal. 77).
635: §.II close: Luther agrees with Augustine in the Ecclesiastical Postil, Septuagesima / Corpus Christi sermons, and on John 6 — see Neodorpius, Orthodox Luther from p. 120.
Stop before §.III (Lutheran double corporal eating / oral restriction).
